keane-bridge.desc: Keane Bridge was built over the Surma in the 1930s and named after Michael Keane, then governor of Assam, when Sylhet was part of that province. Its arched steel spans are the classic picture of Sylhet, especially with the red Ali Amjad clock tower and the riverbank at its northern end. It is now closed to heavy traffic, so it is pleasant to walk across in the evening when the lights come on and boats move below.
blocks: How to get there
In the city centre; a rickshaw from Zindabazar or Bandar Bazar takes a few minutes.
Good to know
Come around sunset and walk the bridge, then sit at the Surma riverfront by the clock tower.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
khadimnagar-national-park.desc: Khadimnagar was declared a national park in 2006 and covers about 679 hectares of hilly forest just beyond Sylhet city. Much of it was once cleared for tea and later replanted with teak, garjan, bamboo, agar and other trees, so it now feels like a young, green forest surrounded by the Kalagul, Burjan and Gulni tea gardens. Forest trails and streams run through it, and monkeys and many birds live here. Most visitors to Sylhet never hear of it, so it stays calm.
blocks: How to get there
From Sylhet city take a CNG via Shahporan toward Khadimnagar (about 30–40 minutes).
Good to know
Walk with a local guide or forest staff, since trails are not well marked. Wear shoes with grip and carry water; watch for leeches after rain.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
jaflong.desc: At Jaflong, the Piyain river runs out of the Indian hills onto a broad bed of stones and sand. Across the border, the green slopes of Meghalaya and the Dawki suspension bridge rise above the water. Boats ferry visitors to the clear shallows at Zero Point, and nearby are Khasi villages with betel-leaf gardens. Stone collection has scarred parts of the area, but the setting remains memorable.
blocks: How to get there
About 1.5–2 hours by bus, CNG or car from Sylhet city along the Tamabil road.
Good to know
Never cross the border markers at Zero Point. Currents can be strong in monsoon, so swim only in shallows and wear a life jacket on boats.

glance: Jara about 200–1,000 BDT each; shashni about 140–350 BDT each (2022 prices)
Citrus stalls at Lalbazar, Sylhet city
sylhet-jara-shashni-citrus.desc: The hills of Sylhet grow citrus found almost nowhere else in the country. Jara is a huge oval citron that can weigh two kilos; shashni smells faintly of cardamom. Sylhetis slice the thick peel as a salad on the side of rice, and squeeze the juice over dal and fish. Expatriate Sylhetis carry them abroad, and stalls in Lalbazar sell them by the piece.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
dibir-haor.desc: Dibir Haor in Jaintiapur upazila is made up of four connected beels, Dibi, Iyam, Harafkata and Kendri, covering roughly 900 acres. From late autumn into winter the water fills with naturally growing red water lilies, which is why locals call it the lal shapla beel. Small boats take you among the flowers, with the hills across the border as a backdrop. The flowers open early and close as the sun gets strong, so mornings are everything here.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Sylhet toward Jaintiapur on the Tamabil road (about 1–1.5 hours), then a CNG or auto to the beel; local boats are hired at the edge.
Good to know
Reach by sunrise or soon after; by late morning the lilies close. Don't pick the flowers. Stay well away from the border line.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
panthumai-waterfall.desc: Panthumai is a village in Gowainghat at the foot of the hills, facing a wide waterfall that tumbles down on the Indian side of the border. You watch it from the Bangladeshi bank of the Piyain stream, with paddy fields and village life all around. Fewer tourists come here than to Bichanakandi, and the scene is especially full in the rainy season.
blocks: How to get there
From Sylhet go to Gowainghat, then by boat or local transport to Panthumai; often combined with Bichanakandi by boat.
Good to know
Do not cross the border. Roads can be muddy in monsoon.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
bichanakandi.desc: Bichanakandi, in Gowainghat, is where several streams from Meghalaya pour out onto a plain of stones, creating a shallow, clear river you can sit in. Mist and waterfalls hang on the Indian hills just beyond. The boat ride from Hadarpar across the haor is part of the journey, and the water is cold and refreshing in summer and rainy months.
blocks: How to get there
From Sylhet city go to Hadarpar via Salutikar (about 1.5 hrs), then a boat to Bichanakandi.
Good to know
Wear sandals with grip; the stones are slippery. Water levels rise quickly after rain in the hills, so leave if the current increases.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
malnicherra-tea-estate.desc: Malnicherra was established in 1854 and is widely described as the first commercial tea garden in the region. Its low hills are covered in neatly clipped tea bushes, shaded by tall trees, with tea workers plucking leaves through much of the year. A short drive from the city centre, it is the easiest place in Sylhet to walk among the tea.
blocks: How to get there
About 15 minutes by CNG from Sylhet city toward the airport road.
Good to know
Stay on paths and ask before photographing workers. Some areas may need permission from the estate office.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
Boat hire per boat (approx. 750–1000 BDT); small entry fee
ratargul-swamp-forest.desc: Ratargul is one of the few freshwater swamp forests in Bangladesh. In the rainy season the forest floor floods several feet deep, and small wooden boats slip between the trunks of hijal, koroch and other water-tolerant trees. The light is green and the water dark and still, and you may spot kingfishers, monkeys and snakes in the branches. In the dry months the water drains away and the forest is much less striking.
blocks: How to get there
From Sylhet city take a CNG to Motorghat (about 1 hr), then a boat into the forest.
Good to know
Go early in the morning; carry an umbrella; keep hands inside the boat because of snakes. Avoid during flood warnings.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
lalakhal.desc: Lalakhal is a stretch of the Sari river in Jaintiapur, famous for its turquoise and emerald colours, which come from minerals and the clear water flowing down from the Meghalaya hills. Engine boats carry visitors upstream from Sarighat, past sandbanks, forest and tea estates toward the border. The colour is most vivid in winter when the water is clearest.
blocks: How to get there
Take the Tamabil road from Sylhet to Sarighat (about 1 hr), then hire an engine boat to Lalakhal.
Good to know
Agree boat fare and duration in advance. Wear a life jacket.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
shah-paran-shrine.desc: Shah Paran is remembered as a nephew and companion of Shah Jalal, who came to Sylhet with him in the 14th century. His shrine stands on a small hillock at Khadim Para on the eastern edge of the city, reached by a flight of steps, with a mosque and a large compound around it. Pilgrims who visit Shah Jalal's shrine usually come here too, and Thursdays and the annual urs are especially crowded.
blocks: How to get there
About 8 km east of Sylhet city centre; take a CNG or local bus toward Shahporan / Khadim Para.
Good to know
Dress modestly and remove shoes at the shrine. Women's access to the inner tomb area may be restricted. Visit Shah Jalal's shrine the same day.

glance: Craft shops in Sylhet city; weaving villages in Balaganj
sylhet-shital-pati.desc: Shital pati, meaning 'cool mat', is woven from thin strips of murta, a reed-like plant that grows in wet areas of Sylhet. The strips are dyed and woven into mats with geometric patterns and sometimes motifs of birds and flowers, and they stay cool to sleep on in hot weather. The traditional art of shital pati weaving of Sylhet was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2017.

glance: Local restaurants around Zindabazar and Ambarkhana, Sylhet city
shatkora-beef.desc: Shatkora is a thick-skinned wild citrus grown in the Sylhet region. Its rind is cut into pieces and cooked with beef or mutton, giving the curry a sharp, fragrant, slightly bitter note unlike anything else in Bangladeshi cooking. It is a pride of Sylheti homes and restaurants, and expatriate Sylhetis carry the fruit to Britain and beyond.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
bholaganj-sada-pathor.desc: At Bholaganj in Companiganj upazila the Dhalai river leaves the Indian hills and spreads over a wide bed of white and grey stones, which gave the spot its name, Sada Pathor (white stone). Boats run from the ghat up to the stone bed, where people wade in the cold, clear water with the green Meghalaya slopes behind. In mid-2025 large-scale looting stripped much of the stone and left bare sand in places; the administration then recovered and dumped back a great deal of it, but the site may not look as it did in older photos. It is still one of the most visited day trips from Sylhet.
blocks: How to get there
From Sylhet city take a CNG or bus to Bholaganj (about 33 km, roughly 1–1.5 hours), then hire a boat from the No. 10 ghat to the stone bed.
Good to know
Currents can be strong in the monsoon; stay in the shallows and wear a life jacket on the boat. Do not cross toward the border markers. Never take stones away.

glance: Restaurants in Zindabazar, Sylhet; especially around iftar time in Ramadan
sylheti-akhni.desc: Akhni is Sylhet's answer to pulao and biryani: rice cooked together with beef or chicken, whole spices and often potatoes, until the grains are coated and flavourful but not heavy. It is made for Eid, weddings and especially for iftar in Ramadan, when big pots appear in homes and shops across the city. It has a lighter touch than Dhaka's biryanis.

glance: Panshi and Panch Bhai restaurants, Zindabazar, Sylhet city
sylheti-bhorta-bhaat-meal.desc: Sylhet's home-style restaurants serve the food Sylheti families eat at home: plain rice with dal and aloo bhorta on the house, then your pick of shutki, haor fish, duck or beef curries, often soured with shatkora or local citrus. Panch Bhai, opened in Zindabazar in 2008, was among the first, and Panshi nearby grew so popular it feeds thousands a day. A filling meal costs little.

glance: 230 km to Sylhet by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
shah-jalal-dargah.desc: Shah Jalal, a 14th-century Sufi saint, is credited in tradition with spreading Islam in the Sylhet region, and his shrine is the spiritual heart of the city. Pilgrims of all backgrounds come to pray and seek blessings. The complex includes a mosque, the tomb, a pond of large catfish that visitors feed, and flocks of grey 'Jalali' pigeons believed to descend from birds he brought.
blocks: How to get there
In Sylhet city at Dargah Gate, easily reached by rickshaw or CNG.
Good to know
Dress modestly and remove shoes. Access for women to the tomb chamber is restricted.

glance: Home-style rice restaurants around Zindabazar, Sylhet city; dried hidol and naga chillies are sold in Lalbazar
sylheti-hidol-bhorta.desc: Hidol (shidol) is small fish fermented in a sealed clay pot until it turns soft and strongly scented. Sylheti cooks roast it and mash it with potato, garlic, onion and a little naga, the region's fiercely hot and fragrant chilli. It is eaten in small pinches with rice, and locals swear a hot hidol bhorta clears a cold. The smell takes getting used to; the taste stays with you.
